title: Changing Complex State Practice
summary: A challenge and walkthrough: finish a form component whose state is an object with three fields (fName, lName, email) so each input updates only its own field. The long if/else-if version of the updater is built deliberately, to be shortened in the next lecture with the spread operator.

concepts.heading: The challenge setup
points: App.jsx is provided with state renamed to `contact` and its setter `setContact`; the initial value is an object with fName, lName and email, all empty strings.
Three inputs and a Submit button sit inside a form. Typing in the first two inputs should fill the h1 greeting; typing in the third should fill a new paragraph beneath the h1.
Concepts to reuse from earlier lessons: object state, updating from the previous state, controlled form inputs, and event handling.
Use the React Developer Tools Components tab to watch the state object change while typing; it is the quickest way to spot a field being wiped or not updating.

concepts.heading: Wiring up the change handler
points: Give every input the same `onChange={handleChange}`. One shared function serves all three inputs. (Tip from the lecture: in VS Code, Option-click places several cursors so the identical attribute is typed once.)

handleChange receives the synthetic event. Destructure only what is needed: `const { name, value } = event.target;`. The `name` attribute on each input (fName, lName, email) tells the handler which field fired; `value` is the text currently typed.
Each input needs a `name` attribute matching the corresponding key in the state object; the comparison in the handler depends on that.

concepts.heading: Updating only the changed field
points: Call `setContact` with a callback that receives the previous state (named prevValue in the solution). Logging the argument is a good way to confirm its shape if unsure.
Inside the callback, branch on `name`: if it is fName, return a full new object with the new `value` for fName while copying lName and email from prevValue; likewise for lName and for email.

Every branch must return a complete object with all three keys. If a key is omitted, that field disappears from state, because the useState setter replaces the whole value rather than merging object properties.
(Extra) This differs from class components, where this.setState shallow-merges the object you pass into the existing state.
This works but repeats near-identical code in three places, which is the motivation for the spread-operator version in the next lecture.

concepts.heading: Controlled inputs and display
points: Add a `value` attribute to each input bound to the state: `contact.fName`, `contact.lName`, `contact.email`. This makes the inputs controlled: React state is the single source of truth, and what appears in the field is always what is stored.
The h1 renders `Hello {contact.fName} {contact.lName}` and the paragraph renders `{contact.email}` as JSX expressions that update on every re-render triggered by setContact.
Verify in DevTools: expanding the App component's hooks shows the contact object; typing in one input changes just that key.

task.name: Changing Complex State: contact form
task.starting_point: App.jsx with a `contact` object state (fName, lName, email), setContact, and a form with three inputs plus an h1 and a paragraph that are not yet connected.
task.goal: Typing in each input updates only its own property in state and shows the first and last name in the h1 and the email in the paragraph beneath it.
steps: Add `onChange={handleChange}` to all three inputs and define handleChange.
Destructure `name` and `value` from `event.target` inside the handler.
Call setContact with a function of the previous state.
Branch on the input name and return a complete new object that replaces just the changed field and copies the other two from the previous state.
Add `value` attributes (contact.fName, contact.lName, contact.email) so the inputs are controlled.
Render contact.fName and contact.lName in the h1 and contact.email in the paragraph.
Check the result with React DevTools.
task.expected_result: Each input can be typed in independently; the greeting and email text update live and no field is cleared when another changes.

pitfalls: Omitting a key in a returned object removes it from state because state is replaced, not merged.
Forgetting the `name` attribute on an input, or a name that does not match the state key and the if-branch string.
Forgetting the `value` attribute leaves the input uncontrolled and out of sync with state.
(Extra) The final else-if has no plain else, so an unexpected name would make the updater return undefined and wipe state.
(Extra) Reading event.target inside the updater callback can fail in older React versions due to event pooling; destructure first, as done here.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Object state in forms': blurb on one state object with several fields and a shared change handler.
Tasks: (1) add onChange and name attributes, (2) destructure name and value, (3) return the full object from setContact, (4) add value to make inputs controlled, (5) show the email in a paragraph.
Starter code: App.jsx with the contact state and unwired inputs.
Interactive demo: live JSON view of the state object beside the form, and a toggle that omits a key to show that field vanishing.
